title: 21 — AI in the Software Development Lifecycle
html:
21 — AI in the Software Development Lifecycle

The premise: AI coding tools are now a normal part of senior engineering practice. The differentiator is no longer whether you use them but whether you use them in a way that raises quality and throughput rather than quietly lowering both.

1. What AI is actually good and bad at

Strong Weak
Boilerplate, scaffolding, wiring Novel algorithms with subtle correctness requirements
Translating between languages/frameworks Deep knowledge of your codebase's implicit conventions
Writing tests for existing code Knowing which tests actually matter
Explaining unfamiliar code Knowing whether the explanation is right (it sounds right either way)
Regex, SQL, config, glob patterns, shell Concurrency correctness, memory ordering, distributed edge cases
Refactoring mechanical patterns at scale Deciding whether to refactor
Documentation and commit messages Architectural judgement and trade-off selection
Exploring an unfamiliar API Distinguishing a deprecated API from a current one
Rubber-ducking a design Understanding your business constraints and history

The asymmetry that matters: AI is best where verification is cheap (a test passes, a type checks, a query returns) and worst where verification is expensive (concurrency, security, architecture). Match your usage and your review depth to the cost of verification.

2. A working model for AI-assisted development

flowchart TD
    A[Task] --> B{Do I understand<br/>the problem and the<br/>desired solution?}
    B -->|No| C["Use AI to EXPLORE:<br/>explain code, list approaches,<br/>find the relevant files"]
    C --> B
    B -->|Yes| D{Is the solution<br/>mechanical or novel?}
    D -->|Mechanical| E["Delegate: give precise context,<br/>constraints, and examples.<br/>Review as a PR."]
    D -->|Novel/subtle| F["Write it yourself;<br/>use AI to review,<br/>test, and find edge cases"]
    E --> G[Verify: read every line,<br/>run tests, check the diff]
    F --> G
    G --> H{Would I defend this<br/>in review as my own work?}
    H -->|No| I[Fix it or rewrite it]
    H -->|Yes| J[Ship]

The governing rule: you own every line you commit. "The AI wrote it" is not a defence in a code review, an incident postmortem, or a security audit. If you can't explain why a line is there, it doesn't go in.

3. Getting good output: context is everything

The quality of AI assistance is dominated by the quality of the context you provide — far more than by prompt phrasing.

Provide Why
The relevant existing code So the output matches your patterns rather than a generic tutorial's
Conventions and constraints "We use Dapper, not EF, in this project"; "target .NET 8"; "no new dependencies"
An example of the target shape One existing, similar, good file is worth ten sentences of description
The actual error output Full stack trace, not a paraphrase
The definition of done "Must handle a null customer and return 404"
What you've already tried Prevents re-suggesting the thing that failed

# Project conventions

## Stack
.NET 9, ASP.NET Core minimal APIs, Dapper (NOT EF Core), Angular 19 standalone, SQL Server.

## Rules
- All SQL lives in `Sql/` as named constants; always parameterised.
- Public async APIs accept and propagate `CancellationToken`.
- Nullable reference types are enabled; no `!` without a justifying comment.
- Domain project has zero external package references.
- Tests: xUnit + NSubstitute; name as `Method_Scenario_ExpectedOutcome`.
- Never add a NuGet/npm package without asking.

## Commands
Build: `dotnet build`  ·  Test: `dotnet test`  ·  Lint frontend: `npm run lint`

A repo-level instructions file is the single highest-leverage investment in AI-assisted development. It moves conventions from tribal knowledge into every AI interaction, for everyone on the team.

4. Reviewing AI-generated code

Review it harder than human code, because it is confidently plausible in ways that human mistakes usually aren't.

The specific failure patterns:

Pattern Example How to catch
Plausible but wrong API A method or overload that doesn't exist, or exists with different semantics Compile it; check the docs; don't trust the signature
Outdated idiom WebClient, BinaryFormatter, ngModule patterns in a standalone project, deprecated flags Compare with current docs and the surrounding code
Silent error swallowing catch { return null; } Grep the diff for empty catches
Missing cancellation/disposal No CancellationToken, no using Checklist item
Ignored edge cases Empty collection, null, zero, concurrent access, timezone Ask explicitly for edge cases, then verify
Subtly wrong concurrency Lock scope, async void, missing await The area where you should be most sceptical
Security gaps Concatenated SQL, missing authorisation, permissive CORS, disabled cert validation Security checklist (file 13)
Hallucinated dependency A plausible package name that doesn't exist — or worse, does exist as a squatted malicious package ("slopsquatting") Verify every new dependency by name and publisher
Over-engineering An interface, factory, and abstract base for one implementation Ask "what does this abstraction buy?"
Tests that assert the bug Tests written from the implementation, so they encode whatever it does Write the assertion yourself, or check it against the requirement

⚠️ Tests generated from the implementation are worse than no tests — they lock in current behaviour, including bugs, and give false confidence. Generate tests from the requirement (or write the assertions yourself and let AI fill in the arrangement).

⚠️ Never paste secrets, customer data, or proprietary algorithms into a tool without an approved data-handling agreement. Know your organisation's policy on what may leave the boundary, and check whether the provider trains on your inputs.

5. Where AI fits across the lifecycle

Phase High-value use Watch out
Requirements Draft user stories, generate edge cases and acceptance criteria, spot ambiguity It invents plausible requirements — validate with the business
Design Enumerate approaches with trade-offs, critique your design, draft an ADR Recommendations skew toward popular/complex; it doesn't know your constraints
Implementation Boilerplate, tests, migrations, mappers, config, regex, SQL See §4
Code review A first pass for bugs, security issues, and missed cases before a human review Noisy on style; can't judge architectural fit. A supplement, not a replacement
Testing Test data builders, parameterised cases, edge-case brainstorming, property definitions Assertions must come from the requirement
Debugging Interpret a stack trace, hypothesise causes, explain unfamiliar code Verify the hypothesis with evidence — it will produce a confident wrong theory
Documentation READMEs, API docs, ADR drafts, changelogs, runbooks Must be checked against reality; stale AI docs are worse than none
Migration/refactor Mechanical transformation across many files, framework upgrades Do it in reviewable chunks with green tests between each
Operations Summarise logs, draft postmortems, generate queries (KQL/SQL/PromQL) Never let it act on production without human confirmation

The highest-ROI uses in practice: (1) tests for existing untested code, (2) understanding an unfamiliar codebase, (3) mechanical refactors at scale, (4) the "I know what I want but not the exact API" gap, (5) first-draft documentation.

6. Team adoption

What works:

  • Commit a repo instructions file and keep it current. Treat it as a shared asset.
  • Share effective prompts and workflows in a team doc — the skill is transferable.
  • Set an explicit review standard: AI-generated code is reviewed to the same or higher bar; the author is the owner.
  • Agree the data policy in writing: which tools, what may be shared, which repos are excluded.
  • Measure the right thing. Not "lines generated" or "acceptance rate" — measure cycle time, change-failure rate, defect escape rate, and review time. If defects rise, the net effect is negative regardless of how fast code appears.
  • Keep juniors learning. Pair AI use with explanation: "have it generate, then explain what each part does and why". The risk is a generation of engineers who can produce code they can't debug.

What doesn't work:

  • Banning it (people use it anyway, without guidance or guardrails).
  • Mandating it (forces bad fits and generates resentment).
  • Measuring adoption instead of outcomes.
  • Letting AI-generated code bypass review because "the tests pass".

7. Risks to manage deliberately

Risk Mitigation
Skill atrophy Deliberately hand-write the hard parts; use AI to review your work, not only to produce it
Verification debt Code accumulates faster than understanding. Cap PR size; require the author to explain the design in the description
Homogenisation Output drifts toward generic patterns and away from your codebase's idioms. Repo instructions + review push back
Licence contamination Generated code may echo licensed source. Use tools with indemnification/filtering; run licence scanning on anything substantial
Dependency hallucination Verify every new package: does it exist, who publishes it, how many downloads, when was it last updated
Security regression AI reproduces insecure patterns from its training data. Run SAST on every PR, no exceptions
Over-trust in explanations An AI explanation of unfamiliar code is a hypothesis. Verify against behaviour before acting on it
Confidential data leakage Approved tools only; know the retention terms; never paste secrets or customer data

8. Building AI features into your product (as opposed to using AI to build)

If you're adding an AI capability to your application, the engineering discipline from file 20 applies. The additional product-level considerations:

Consideration Guidance
Is AI the right solution? If deterministic logic does the job, use it. Users prefer predictable software
Failure mode What happens when the model is wrong, slow, or unavailable? Design that path first, not last
Trust and transparency Say it's AI-generated. Show sources. Make it easy to verify and to correct
Human in the loop For anything consequential, the model drafts and a person approves
Feedback capture Thumbs up/down with the full context logged — this becomes your eval set
Cost per user Model it before launch; a viral feature with unbounded token use is a financial incident
Latency budget Stream, or show progress. A 20-second blank screen is a broken feature regardless of the answer quality
Regulatory Automated decisions affecting individuals may require explanation and contestability (file 19 §8.5)
Evaluation A CI eval suite before launch, and online monitoring after (file 20 §6)

A useful rule for scoping: ship the version where the AI assists a human before the version where it replaces the human. The assisted version is lower risk, generates the data and evals you need, and usually captures most of the value.

9. Checklist & interview angles

Personal practice checklist

  • Repo instructions file exists and is current
  • I provide relevant code, conventions, and constraints — not just a one-line ask
  • I read and understand every generated line before committing
  • I verify APIs and dependencies actually exist and are current
  • Tests come from requirements, not from the implementation
  • Security-sensitive and concurrency code gets extra scrutiny (or I write it myself)
  • No secrets, customer data, or proprietary IP pasted into unapproved tools
  • PRs stay small enough to review properly
  • I can explain the design decisions in the PR description in my own words

Team checklist

  • Written data-handling policy for AI tools
  • Same-or-higher review bar for AI-generated code; author is the owner
  • SAST, dependency scanning, and licence scanning in CI
  • Outcome metrics tracked (cycle time, change-failure rate, defect escape), not adoption metrics
  • Juniors are learning, not just accepting completions
  • Shared prompt/workflow knowledge base

🔍 Interview angles

  • How do you use AI in your workflow? Give a specific, honest answer with a boundary: what you delegate, what you don't, and how you verify. The expected signal is judgement, not enthusiasm.
  • How do you review AI-generated code? Name the specific failure patterns (§4) — hallucinated APIs and packages, outdated idioms, swallowed errors, missing cancellation, concurrency subtleties, tests that assert the implementation.
  • What are the risks for a team? Verification debt, security regression, skill atrophy, dependency hallucination, data leakage — with a mitigation for each.
  • When would you not use it? Novel algorithms with subtle correctness requirements, security-critical code, concurrency, and anywhere I can't cheaply verify the result.
  • Has it changed how you work? The useful answer: it compressed the mechanical work, which shifted more of my time to design, review, and verification — so the bottleneck moved from typing to judgement.
